title: ‘Our History Is Better Than Anybody Else’s’
text:
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. 

 F or years now, Donald Trump and the MAGA movement have cast the United States as the heir to and defender of Western civilization. In the second Trump administration, this sort of grandiose rhetoric has increased; the administration presents itself as the lone bulwark against the barbarians at the gates who would annihilate everything good about the world.

 “Our lineage and our legacy hails back to Athens, to Rome,” Stephen Miller, Trump’s longtime adviser and new chief of staff, said at the funeral for the assassinated conservative activist Charlie Kirk. “Our ancestors built the cities. They produced the art and architecture. They built the industry” that pulled “us out of the caves and the darkness into the light.”

 Secretary of State Marco Rubio gave a similar speech a month ago, in actual Athens. “The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man. And it began here, with the first men and women of the West,” Rubio announced. “This was the foundation of the Western mind: Our math, our science, our medicine. Our philosophy, ethics, and religion. It paved the way for the Gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom.”

 Certainly one can see the legacy of ancient societies in how we live today—the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle, the many denominations of Christianity descended from its embrace by the Romans, the Romance languages spoken from Santiago to Sambava. The American Founders took inspiration from antiquity, a debt you can see in the mighty structures surrounding the National Mall.

 Yet what many conservatives describe as Western civilization is not so much a consistent historical fact as an ideological project, one that has long been used to demonstrate the inherent superiority of certain people—white people—in order to legitimize a claim to power and dominance. Europe and the West began to emerge as coherent political identities relatively recently, in the early 17th century; they are not timeless, immutable concepts.

 [ Adam Serwer: The GOP’s message to immigrants ] 

 Some conservative-media figures have been explicit about what they mean by Western civilization. The right-wing podcaster Matt Walsh described Americans as “the best innovators, lawmakers, scientists, artists, athletes, thinkers, and fighters in the entire world. We’re not a ‘melting pot’ or a mishmash of inferior, squabbling cultures.” If the country could just “evict anti-American invaders,” it could go back to being “an unstoppable force advancing the interests of civilization, without apology.” That apology is the problem: America, and by extension the West, has grown weak because it has stopped asserting its superiority over others as a means of honoring its inheritance.

 “Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional,” Rubio said, and that shame threatened to condemn Americans to “a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.”

 This sort of argument plays well at rallies, and conservatives have long been trying to institutionalize and intellectualize it through college curricula. But it is based on an outdated historiography that takes into account neither how these ancient societies saw themselves nor their relationship to the societies around them. It is a bedtime story about being the bestest boys who ever lived—in short, a myth. And at the core of this myth is the idea that human progress is the product of isolation and ethnic homogeneity, rather than a collective endeavor.

 It is one thing to take inspiration from past societies, and another entirely to claim their accomplishments as your own personal inheritance. This is a race-based argument, as if the accomplishment of a Caesar, an Alexander, or a Napoleon belonging to all white people carries any more weight than the average Eagles fan saying, “We won the Super Bowl.” There is no question that Greek and Roman texts from antiquity—Aristotle’s Poetics , Cicero’s speeches, Sappho’s poetry—are worthy of study. Concepts associated with Western civilization, such as democracy, freedom of speech, religious tolerance, and capitalism, have undoubtedly shaped the modern world. But appreciating the canonical texts of what Rubio and others refer to as Western civilization is not the same as telling the story they want to tell, which is that virtually every human achievement of note was attained by Europeans.

 T he culprit for the West’s loss of confidence, many conservatives believe, is the “woke” university. Richard Nixon said, “The professors are the enemy,” half a century ago, but educational polarization—the drift of college-educated voters to the left and non-college-educated voters to the right—has lent the critique a new urgency. The former Trump adviser Steve Bannon recently told The Boston Globe that universities were the only reason Democrats are “able to compete with us.” One response is to try to force students to learn a particular version of the story of Western civilization, a version that is not a neutral account of concepts such as capitalism, democracy, and Christianity, but an argument that capitalism, democracy, and Christianity are superior to the heathen cultures of foreign barbarians.

 Republican legislatures and administrators in states such as Texas and Florida have moved to reorient university curricula toward this vision. The Democrats’ sweep of state offices in Texas may halt some of these changes, but unwinding them will take time, while the general trend in red states is likely to continue. In 2023, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis championed legislation to “ensure Florida’s public universities and colleges are grounded in the history and philosophy of Western Civilization.” William Inboden, the provost at the University of Texas at Austin, has called for a renewed commitment “to the American people, our constitutional order, Western civilization, and the classical liberal arts.” The shift at UT Austin and elsewhere coincided with the slashing of courses related to race and gender—perhaps because these subjects threaten to complicate the preferred narrative of Western civilization.

 Conservatives have tried to present this effort as “depoliticizing” scholarship, in Inboden’s description. But historians are always making new discoveries or reinterpreting old ones. What these conservatives are really attempting to do is stop the process of revision and rediscovery in favor of past interpretations that promote the idea that America is the successor to the great civilizations of antiquity, and is thus entitled to dominate the world in the name of humanity.

 “One powerful tool of legitimacy is invoking a past golden age,” the historian Ada Palmer writes in Inventing the Renaissance . “Golden ages are mythical constructions (the events are real but the golden ageness is invented), so it’s easy to claim you are the true successor, even if you have little historical connection.”

 The question, though, is legitimacy for what? America’s Founders were arguably some of the original Roman-statue guys: Grounding American independence in the Greco-Roman world allowed the colonists to smooth over denominational divides and justify their own freedoms alongside the institution of slavery and the dispossession of Native Americans. John Stuart Mill argued that “despotism is a legitimate mode of government in dealing with barbarians, provided the end be their improvement.” Convenient for the despot!

 What this narrative misses is the fact that the idea of separate civilizations at all is a relatively young one. In How the World Made the West , the classical historian Josephine Quinn identifies the idea as originating in the 19th century, alongside, not coincidentally, the age of colonization. European nations that sought to subjugate other peoples found it convenient to posit that those peoples were inferior, and that despotism was thus justified. The world was hardly harmonious before that; war and ethnic strife were common. But the concept of civilization was generally thought of as singular, Quinn writes, as in human civilization.

 The narrative of separate civilizations was later adapted for the Cold War, and revived for the post-9/11 era. Now it has been resurrected as self-soothing rhetoric for a right-wing-populist project, a kind of collectivist monarchist belief that white people—or, in euphemism, “the West”—are born to rule. But we know now that the world of antiquity was much more interconnected than was previously believed. As Quinn writes, human civilization is a story of “exchange between people from different places and cultures,” and “without it there wouldn’t be much of a story at all.”

 Ancient Greece took inspiration from the Egyptians to its south and the Phoenicians (from whom they drew their alphabet) and Assyrians to its east. The Iliad and The Odyssey , Quinn writes, “show us that Greek speakers of that era still chose to sing of international kingdoms, intercontinental war, and voyages across broad seas.” Greek coins and Roman amphorae have been found in India, where Alexander led his army and where Greek kingdoms existed for centuries afterward. Augustus’s legions marched south along the Nile until halted by the queen of Kush, a kingdom that had been in contact with the Greeks for generations and had provided Egypt with many of its rulers. We do math with Arabic numerals, and the concept of zero was invented by an Indian mathematician in the seventh century. The main religion of Western civilization, Christianity, was founded by an Aramaic-speaking rabbi in West Asia.

 Agriculture, philosophy, literacy, navigation, metalworking—all of these advanced in antiquity because goods and people traveled, and ideas traveled with them. “What are called Western values—freedom, rationality, justice, and tolerance—are not only or originally western,” Quinn writes, “and the West itself is in large part a product of long-standing links with a much larger network of societies, to south and north as well as east.” I am not arguing that these societies were “superior” to Western ones—only that societies learn from contact with one another rather than through ethnic purity and enforced segregation.

 Taking the Greeks and Romans as the origin of Western civilization is an ideological project, not a historical one, a little bit like a posthumous baptism. The ancients largely did not see race the way many of our contemporaries do: as an immutable biological category. Projecting that conception backwards is like imagining that Xerxes scrolled through updates on the Battle of Thermopylae on his iPhone. The stereotypes that ancients did embrace rarely line up with contemporary views. Aristotle, for example, did not consider the Greek city-states part of Europe, whose population he dismissed as inferior. People who lived in Europe’s colder regions, he wrote, were “full of spirit but inferior with regard to intelligence and skill,” adding that they lacked “civic organization and the ability to rule their neighbours.”

 Rome, meanwhile, as the classicist Naoíse Mac Sweeney writes in The West , “ gloried in the idea of itself as a mongrel nation,” tracing its mythical origin, in Virgil’s epic Aeneid , not to Northern Europe, but to Troy, in Asia. As Quinn writes, “As late as the first century BCE some Roman geographers were still unsure whether Europe and Africa were separate continents.” That’s understandable, considering that North African grain kept the empire fed, and “by the 180s CE nearly a third of Roman senators were of African origin.” Basically everyone in the Roman empire was a “polyglot,” Palmer writes. “One heard all sorts of languages in the streets of Rome: Aramaic, Hebrew, etc., with Greek serving as a lingua Franca.”

 Many of the texts that tell us about these worlds, the supposed blueprints of Western civilization, might have been lost during the Middle Ages, Mac Sweeney points out, if they had not been preserved in places such as the House of Wisdom, the great library in Baghdad that drew scholars from all over the world.

 C laiming descent from the Roman empire is an ancient, and global, pastime. The citizens of the Eastern Roman empire called themselves Romans, never Byzantines. Once they were defeated by the Ottomans, the sultan took the title kayser-i-rum , or “Caesar of Rome.” The czar of Russia is similarly derived from caesar . Ivan III went so far as to marry the Byzantine princess Sophia Palaiologina to bolster Moscow’s claim to being the “Third Rome.” The Holy Roman Empire put it right there in the name.

 So many of Trump’s political strategies are intended to make the same case: the “Western civilization” speeches; the landmarks he names after himself; the proposals to colonize Greenland and Canada; the calls for public executions of enemies; the grand ballroom and arch in Washington, D.C. It is a regime legitimization tactic dreamed up by a 10-year-old who wants to grow up to be Roman emperor.

 [ Listen: Why America isn’t Rome (and why that matters) ] 

 MAGA’s nostalgia for this outdated historiography has been used to back up arguments that demographic change, expansions of civic equality, and political transition threaten the advance of civilization, instead of being the prerequisites for it. Better to throw up walls, tariff your allies and enemies alike, pursue mass deportation, defund and censor scholarship, and wage wars to demonstrate your superior might. In a speech to the Federalist Society this month dismissing the legitimacy of the International Criminal Court, Rubio quoted the Roman general Pompey: “Stop quoting laws to men with swords.”

 John Adams was fond of quoting a different Roman, Cicero: “ cedant arma togae ,” or “let arms give way to togas.” The Founders idealized the Roman republic —not the Roman empire, which they saw as a cautionary tale about the death of free societies. Pompey’s quote foreshadows that death—and his own beheading. Rubio’s praise for the rule of arms over the rule of law identifies him as the kind of man the Founders thought had destroyed the republic, instead of defending it. Thomas Jefferson called appeals to force like Rubio’s “the vital principle and immediate parent of despotism.”

 Judging by the results of the midterms, voters don’t see the Trump era as a new golden age. This administration does share some qualities with ancient Rome—a predilection for oligarchy , public executions , and losing wars to Persia , to name just a few. But the idea of America as the apex of civilization will persist long after MAGA is gone, because people’s identities and the status they derive from those identities are important to them. Stories like these stick because they convey a simple message: We are better . Maybe the we is “Americans.” Maybe it’s Europeans. Maybe it’s men, heterosexuals, Christians, or conservatives. As Rubio put it: “I never said our history is perfect. I have only said our history is better than anybody else’s.”

 But as Quinn writes, civilizations do not advance through isolation; they advance through exchange. There is no ancient Greece without Phoenicia and Mesopotamia, no ancient Rome without Egypt and Anatolia, and, I would add, no America without African gold and labor . Clearly, these exchanges are not always pleasant or mutually beneficial. War, genocide, slavery, and exploitation are cornerstones of the human experience. Antiquity was not a tolerant, multiracial paradise, but neither is the story of humanity a hero’s journey with the Great White Man as protagonist. Given how human civilization actually advances, the fixation on purity and uniformity is self-destructive. Without change, without dynamism, societies are doomed to decay. Rather than preserving “civilization,” you suffocate your own society like a candle flame in a bell jar.
